transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for fitting me in. I, um, I hope I'm not wasting your time. 

I suppose what brings me in is... well, my sleep has become completely unmoored lately. I tried to manage it myself, of course, because I didn't want to make a fuss. At first, it actually seemed quite fine. I would be up after just two or three hours, but I was feeling completely ready to go—sitting at my desk drafting plans and getting quite a lot done. It really didn't feel like a problem then. 

But lately... well, it's changed. Now I just lie awake for hours before dawn. My stomach gets terribly tight, and there's just no sense of rest at all anymore. 

I hope that's the sort of thing I should be bringing up? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information to start with.
Do you notice feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things during the day, or have you been feeling this way mostly at night when trying to sleep?

Well, it's... it's during the day, too, I'm afraid. I really don't want to sound ungrateful or dramatic, because I know I have a very comfortable life, but... yes, I suppose I have been losing interest in things. 

It's a bit embarrassing to admit, really. I used to spend whole afternoons at the museum, or I'd completely lose myself in my photography and cooking. But lately... well, I'll look at my camera sitting on the shelf, or think about going down to the bridge table, and I just... I feel absolutely nothing. Nothing except, I suppose, the sheer effort it would take to just pretend I'm enjoying it. 

I do try to keep up appearances so I don't worry my friends, but it's become quite difficult. Does that answer what you were asking, Doctor? I want to make sure I'm giving you what you need to know.
Have you experienced any periods where your mood was unusually high, expansive, or irritable, where you felt overly confident or didn’t need much sleep?

Well... yes, I suppose there was a time recently that might fit that description. I hesitate to even bring it up, because I don't want you to think I'm a difficult person. I'm usually quite even-tempered, really. 

But a few weeks ago, I felt... well, almost brilliantly optimistic. It was actually quite wonderful at first. I felt like every little obstacle in my life was completely trivial, like I had it all perfectly figured out. I felt very capable, you know? 

The embarrassing part—and I do apologize if this sounds awful—is that my patience wore terribly thin. If anyone questioned my ideas or suggested I slow down, I... well, I snapped at them. I felt like they were trying to sabotage me, as if I were the only sensible man in the room and they were all just dragging their feet. I feel terrible about it now, of course. It's not how I like to treat people. 

Is that the sort of thing you were looking for? I hope I'm not painting too dreadful a picture of myself.
How long did that elevated mood last—was it for a few days, a week, or longer?

Oh... well, I suppose it was quite a bit longer than a week, I'm afraid. It's actually rather embarrassing to admit, really, but... it went on for about five months. 

You see, there was a... well, a bit of an investment loss right before all of that started. I probably shouldn't have let it get to me as much as I did, I know better than that, but for those five months, I just wasn't living like my usual retired self at all. Everything just completely revolved around trying to undo the damage. I was so dreadfully focused on fixing it, making these grand plans, and that's why I was so sharp with people. 

I do hope I don't sound completely unreasonable, Doctor. I know five months is a terribly long time to be acting like that. Does that answer your question properly? I just want to be sure I'm giving you the right timeline.

During that time when your mood was elevated and you felt very confident and focused, did you also notice any other changes in yourself — like feeling like you didn't need much sleep, talking more than usual, having thoughts race through your head, or taking on more projects or activities than you normally would?

Well... yes, I suppose I did take on quite a few more projects than usual. I really hope people didn't find me too overbearing—I certainly didn't mean to be a nuisance to anyone. I just wanted to be useful, you see. 

But looking back, it was rather excessive for someone who is supposed to be enjoying a quiet retirement. I actually started... well, I began mentoring multiple different companies all at once. And I was drafting these rather elaborate fundraising campaigns, arranging business lunches with half the town... it was far, far beyond what I would normally ever take on these days. 

I just felt so incredibly driven to get things done and fix my situation. I hope that doesn't make me sound completely unreasonable, taking all of that on at my age. Does that give you what you were looking for, Doctor? I want to be sure I'm answering you properly and giving you the right details.

During that time when you were mentoring several companies and felt very driven, did you also experience other changes such as a decreased need for sleep, thoughts racing through your mind, speaking more quickly or more than usual, or engaging in activities that had serious consequences or were out of character for you?

Oh dear... well, I suppose since you ask about my thoughts... I do hope you won't think I was completely losing my faculties. I've always prided myself on being a very organized, deliberate thinker. But during those months... yes, I suppose my thoughts were moving rather briskly. 

It's a bit embarrassing to admit, but my mind would just... well, it would jump constantly. I’d be figuring out a portfolio strategy, and then instantly my brain would snap to potential donors, and then on to museum exhibits, and then to some entirely new business idea. It was all happening so incredibly fast that... well, I could barely finish speaking one sentence before the next one took over. 

I must have been so terribly exhausting to converse with. I really hope I didn't burden my colleagues and friends too much with all that scattered thinking. I just had so much enthusiasm, you see, and I wanted to share it all. Is that... is that what you mean by racing thoughts, Doctor? I do hope I'm answering your questions properly and giving you what you need.

During that time when you were mentoring multiple companies, having racing thoughts, and feeling very confident, did your behavior become so extreme or impairing that someone suggested you needed help, or did you ever feel like you were losing control of your thoughts or actions?

Well... oh dear, this is probably the hardest part to talk about. I really, really hate to admit this, Doctor, because I've always been the one to take care of things, you know? I've always been so reliable. 

But... yes, I suppose things did get a bit out of hand. My wife, bless her, she's had to... well, she's had to take over the finances entirely. And she insists on staying with me now, just to... just for safety, she says. I know I must have worried her terribly, and I feel just awful about it. 

And my commitments... I've always been so dedicated to the museum and the arts council, but lately, I... well, I haven't been showing up reliably at all. Even my friends, I've been quite absent. I suppose I just got so caught up in everything else that I let my real responsibilities slip. 

I'm so ashamed to have let people down like that. It's really not like me at all. I hope you don't think too poorly of me for letting things get to this point. I'm just trying to be completely honest with you... does that help explain how things have been? I want to make sure I'm giving you the full picture, even the parts I'm not proud of.
Would you say that during that five-month period, your mood was consistently elevated or irritable most of the day, nearly every day, and that this was a noticeable change from your usual self?

Well... yes, I suppose it was quite a change from my usual self. I really hope I don't come across as terribly difficult or unpleasant when I explain this, Doctor. I've always tried to be an agreeable person. 

But for weeks on end, I just felt... well, almost brilliantly optimistic. It was quite wonderful at first, actually. I felt as if every obstacle in my path was just entirely trivial, like I could solve anything. I was just so eager to help and fix things, you see. 

But... and this is the part I'm rather ashamed of... if anyone questioned my plans or suggested I slow down, I'm afraid I wasn't my usual polite self at all. I would... well, I would snap at them. I felt like they were trying to sabotage me, and I'd act as if I were the only sensible man in the room. 

It was very out of character for me, and I feel just awful about how irritable I became with people who were only trying to help. I do hope you can understand that I didn't mean to be so cross with everyone. Does that answer your question about my mood, Doctor? I want to make sure I'm giving you exactly what you need to know.

After that five-month period of elevated mood and increased activity, did you experience a time when you felt extremely down, had persistent sadness, or lost interest in nearly all activities for most of the day, more days than not?

Oh, my... well, yes. It's... it's a bit difficult to talk about, to be perfectly honest. I do hope you won't think I'm just being lazy or ungrateful for all the wonderful things in my life. I really have tried to keep up appearances, I promise you.

But after all that excitement faded... things just went rather dark. And the hardest part is... well, the things I usually love so much, they just don't seem to matter anymore. I'm almost too embarrassed to say it, because it sounds so dreadful, but... I used to spend whole afternoons at the museum, or I'd lose myself completely in my photography or cooking a lovely meal. I've always been so passionate about those things. 

But lately... I just look at my camera, or I think about sitting down at the bridge table with my friends, and I feel absolutely nothing. Nothing at all, except... except how exhausting it would be to just pretend I was enjoying myself. I feel terrible even admitting that out loud. It's so unfair to my friends and my wife. I do try to put on a brave face, but it's just so empty inside. 

Is that... is that the sort of thing you're asking about, Doctor? I hope I'm not complaining too much. I just want to be sure I'm giving you the right information so you can help me.

Before this five-month period ended, did you notice a time when you had at least three of the following: feeling like you didn't need much sleep, talking more or faster than usual, having racing thoughts, being more involved in activities than usual, taking unnecessary risks, or being unusually distracted or irritable?

Oh, dear... yes, I suppose I did experience some of those things. I really hope it doesn't sound like I was just being chaotic or disorganized, because I've always prided myself on being quite focused. 

But during that time... well, my thoughts were just moving so terribly fast. I'd be thinking about a portfolio strategy, and then suddenly I'd be on to potential donors, and then museum exhibits, and then some completely new business idea. It was all just... tumbling over itself. I could barely finish speaking one sentence before the next thought just completely took over my mind. 

I know it must have been quite exhausting for anyone trying to have a conversation with me, and I feel just awful if I was overwhelming people. I really was just trying to be productive with all these ideas I had. Does that... does that make sense, Doctor? I hope I'm explaining it clearly enough for you.

Would you say that the five-month period you described was clearly different from your usual mood when you are not depressed, and was it sustained enough that others could clearly see you were acting out of character?

Well... yes, I suppose it was quite obvious to everyone around me. I really hope my wife hasn't been too terribly burdened by it all, I always try to be a good partner to her. 

But for about five months... right after we had that rather unfortunate investment loss... I just wasn't living like my usual retired self at all. I know I should have just accepted the loss gracefully, like a sensible person would. But instead, everything just revolved around trying to undo the damage. I was entirely consumed by it, day and night. 

I feel so foolish admitting that I let it take over my life like that. I know it must have looked so strange to our friends, seeing me act so... intensely, for such a long stretch of time. I really do try to maintain a sense of decorum, you know? 

I hope I'm not painting too dreadful a picture of myself, Doctor. Is that the kind of timeline you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right details.

After that five-month period of high energy and racing thoughts, did you go on to experience a time when you felt persistently down or hopeless for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Oh, yes... yes, it's been quite a long time, actually. I feel terrible even admitting it, because I know I should have just pulled myself together by now. I really do try to stay positive, I promise you. 

But... well, ever since all those big plans of mine fell apart, I've just been in this awful slump. It's been about nine months now of just feeling so low, and so incredibly guilty about everything. I've mostly just been withdrawing from everyone, which I know is so rude of me. I really don't mean to be a burden or a bad friend. 

Nine months is such a terribly long time to feel this way, isn't it? I hope you don't think I'm just wallowing in it. I really am trying my best. Does that answer your question, Doctor? I want to be sure I'm giving you the exact timeline you need.

This adds to previous candidates F33.9 (Major depressive disorder, unspecified) and F43.22 (Adjustment disorder with depressed mood). Further assessment is needed to rule between these conditions.

The patient reported a prolonged elevated mood lasting five months, which rules out F43.22 (Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood) as the duration and mood episodes are more consistent with a bipolar or recurrent depressive disorder. F31.3 (Bipolar Disorder, Current Episode Manic, Mild or No Psychotic Features) remains due to the presence of a manic-like episode, while F33.9 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder, Unspecified) is still possible given the depressive symptoms. Further clarification is needed to determine if the manic episode meets criteria for Bipolar I or if the depressive episodes are recurrent enough to support F33.9.

The patient reported a prolonged elevated mood lasting five months with increased goal-directed activity, racing thoughts, decreased need for sleep, and significant impairment (e.g., loss of normal responsibilities, financial oversight transferred to spouse). This supports a possible bipolar disorder (F31.3). However, the presence of persistent loss of interest, anhedonia, and insomnia also supports major depressive disorder, recurrent, unspecified (F33.9). Further evaluation is needed to determine if the mood episodes meet full criteria for bipolar I or if the elevated mood was secondary to depression or another condition.
